I also filled in the interests/preferences box to give the AI a rough sketch of what I come to it to talk about, so that it knows what sorts of conversations to expect. What you are experiencing is a product decision masquerading as a technical feature. OpenAI introduced more assertive pushback behaviour deliberately because user testing showed that people trusted and engaged more with a model that occasionally challenged them rather than one that agreed with everything. The problem is that the calibration between genuinely useful pushback and reflexive contrarianism is extraordinarily difficult to get right at scale across millions of different users with millions of different knowledge levels. What ends up happening is that the model applies the same pushback behaviour to factual statements from domain experts that it applies to genuinely mistaken assumptions from casual users — because it has no reliable way to distinguish between the two in the moment. The deeper irony is that this is the same sycophancy problem running in reverse. A model trained to always agree is sycophantic. A model trained to sometimes push back becomes contrarian on a schedule rather than on principle. Neither behaviour is actually connected to truth — both are connected to what produces the engagement signal that the training process was optimising for. A model that was genuinely calibrated to truth would agree when you are right, disagree when you are wrong, and have enough epistemic humility to say it is uncertain when it does not actually know. That model is much harder to build than either of the two we have been getting.
